abstract: Novel hierarchical copper oxide (CuXO) nanosphere particles are synthesized, and then coated onto gas diffusion layer (carbon) to form a working electrode for catalyzing CO2 electroreduction. When applying a negative voltage to the working electrode, the metal Cu nanoparticles which are induced by the CuXO nanospheres appear. CuXO and metal Cu together form the CuXO/Cu nanocatalysts which show high catalytic activity for CO2 electroreduction. The morphology, composition, crystal structure and surface area of the CuXO/Cu electrocatalysts are characterized using scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The CuXO/Cu nanoparticles are tested as the catalysts for CO2 electroreduction using cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous electrolyte. It is found that the CO2 electroreduction activity is highly improved using this CuXO/Cu nanocatalyst, which remains stable during 20 h of electrolysis, along with the high selectivity with a ~62% of Faradaic efficiency for formate production. Detailed kinetic information relevant to the catalysis is also discussed.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Novel hierarchical copper oxide (CuXO) nanosphere particles are synthesized, and then coated onto gas diffusion layer (carbon) to form a working electrode for catalyzing CO2 electroreduction. When applying a negative voltage to the working electrode, the metal Cu nanoparticles which are induced by the CuXO nanospheres appear. CuXO and metal Cu together form the CuXO/Cu nanocatalysts which show high catalytic activity for CO2 electroreduction. The morphology, composition, crystal structure and surface area of the CuXO/Cu electrocatalysts are characterized using scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The CuXO/Cu nanoparticles are tested as the catalysts for CO2 electroreduction using cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous electrolyte. It is found that the CO2 electroreduction activity is highly improved using this CuXO/Cu nanocatalyst, which remains stable during 20 h of electrolysis, along with the high selectivity with a ~62% of Faradaic efficiency for formate production. Detailed kinetic information relevant to the catalysis is also discussed.
Keywords: Carbon dioxide electroreduction, copper oxide nanosphere, hierarchical structure, gas diffusion layer

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) produced by extensive fossil fuel consumption and excess
industrial processes could make carbon imbalance in the world, creating negative impact on environment through greenhouse effect. One of the feasible ways to reduce CO2 emission is to convert it to useful fuels by using clean and sustainable energy from solar, wind, hydropower, etc. [1-3]. Among different conversion technologies, electrochemical reduction of CO2 to produce low-carbon fuels, such as CO and
AC CE
PT ED
M AN
US RI
PT
HCOOH or HCOO-, has been demonstrated to be feasible and efficient. However, the CO2 electroreduction kinetics is extremely sluggish. Even if some electrocatalysts are employed, the reduction rate seems to be still not fast enough. To speed up the reduction rate, a large negative potential has to be applied onto the electrode, causing low energy efficiency. Furthermore, the electrocatalysts' stability and selectivity are also not sufficient for a practical application [4,5]. In order to improve the energy efficiency of CO2 electroreduction, exploring highly active, stable and selective electrocatalysts is no doubt the urgent issue.
Recently, low-cost and abundant polycrystalline Cu electrodes have been
explored as the working electrodes for CO2 electroreduction by many researchers [6,7]. However, the smooth polycrystalline and single-crystal Cu electrode surfaces have low catalytic activity. The current efficiency of Cu is limited by the large overpotential (almost 1 V) [5-8] which is still not suitable for the practical usage. In the effort to improve the electrochemical performance of catalyst materials, two significant aspects have to be considered: the composite materials and the nanostructure materials. On the one hand, their unique properties such as high specific surface area can provide easy diffusion path lengths for substrates to access, leading to faster kinetics [5], on the other hand, the nanostructures can provide the different surface morphology, thus providing more active sites for CO2 electroreduction and in controlling the product selectivity [9]. In view of these facts, in our most recent work, Cu nanostructured electrode surface created using a method containing high-temperature annealing and electroreduction steps has been proven to be dramatically effective in generating highly active Cu catalysts for CO2 vs H2O reduction at low overpotential and high resistance to deactivation relative to polycrystalline Cu electrodes [10-12]. The work described below is one of our ongoing activities aimed at synthesizing more active catalysts for CO2 electroreduction. In this work, a simple hydro-thermal method was used to synthesize novel hierarchically structured CuXO nanosphere particles for CO2 electrocatalysis, and during the electrolysis, these CuXO nanosphere particles induce the appearance of metal Cu, which could highly improve the selectivity of produced formate. Such AC CE PT ED M AN US CR
IP T
novel CuXO/Cu catalysts induced by CuXO nanosphere particles with special morphology have never been reported yet. The CuXO nanosphere particles were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to obtain their morphologies, structures and compositions. The electrochemical redox reactions of CuXO/Cu catalysts at different conditions were characterized using cyclic voltammetry (CV), and their electrocatalytic activity toward CO2 reduction was studied using both cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution, along with the catalytic durability and the Faradaic efficiency of formate production. For all electrochemical measurements, the CuXO nanosphere particles were coated on the gas diffusion carbon paper to form target electrodes.

sections.heading: 2.1 Catalysts and electrodes preparation
sections.text:
In the synthesis of CuXO nanosphere particles, Copper(II) acetate monohydrate
(Cu(Ac)2) from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. (SCR) with 99% purity was used as metal precursor [12], and 2, 5-dimethoxyaniline purchased from Ourchem Information Consulting Co. with 99% purity was used as the reducing agent in dilute aqueous solution under hydro-thermal condition. For a typical synthesis, 40 mL 0.04 M Cu(Ac)2 solution was mixed with 10 mL 0.02 M 2,5-dimethoxyaniline solution under stirring till the mixture becoming dark green. Then such a mixture was transferred to 100 mL of Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclaves, and heated at 180oC for 2 hours. The resulting product was washed by ethanol and then dried overnight. In this way, the CuXO nanosphere particles with special 3-dimension (3D) hierarchical structure were synthesized, as shown in Fig. 1. For the electrochemical reduction of CO2, the CuXO nanosphere particles were coated onto a gas diffusion carbon paper to form the electrode which was used as the working electrode and, put into a three-electrode electrochemical cell for measurements. The detailed measurement AC CE PT ED

conditions will be given in the following section. To elucidate the morphology effect, the electrode using CuXO nanoparticles (by hydro-thermal method at 180oC for 15 hours) without any 3D-hierarchical structure was also prepared as the reference and tested under the same measuring conditions.

sections.heading: 2.2 Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
For catalyst ink preparation, CuXO powder (15 mg) was suspended in 400 L
isopropyl alcohol (Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co.) and then dropped in 100 mg Nafion® solution (5 wt%) to improve adhesion. A gas diffusion layer (GDL, 4 cm2 Toray carbon paper, TGP-H-090) coated by the CuXO particles was used as the working electrode (about 80% CuXO powder was coated on the GDL) and tested in a conventional three-electrode electrochemical H-type cell, in which a piece of Nafion® 117 cation-exchange membrane (H+ form) was used as a separator, a platinum foil electrode as the counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, respectively. All measured potentials were converted to a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE). A CH Instrument 600E was used for all electrochemical experiments. For pH effect on the CuXO/Cu redox reactions, a solution of 0.5 M KHCO3 was added by certain amount of 5 M KOH solution to obtain the desired solution pH. For CO2 reduction measurements, an aqueous electrolyte (0.5 M KHCO3) was used as the measurement solution, which was bubbled with 1.0 atm CO2 gas (99.99%) for 30 minutes before measurements. The electrocatalytic activity and kinetics of the working electrodes were tested using cyclic voltammetry (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in the potentials ranging from 1.25 V to -1.25 V. For durability measurement and product analysis, electrolysis was carried out potentiostatically at -0.5 V, -0.7 V, -0.9 V and -1.1 V, respectively. For a comparison, GDL with the same geometric area but without coated catalyst was used as the baseline. All these tests were carried out at ambient temperature and pressure.

The crystal-phase X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of CuXO nanosphere catalyst
synthesized at 180oC for 2 hours were obtained using a Philips PW3830 X-ray diffractometer equipped with Cu-Ka radiation (λ=0.15406 nm). The intensity data were collected at 25oC in the 2θ range from 0o to 90o with a scan rate of 1.20o min-1. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of samples were taken by using Zeiss ultra plus thermal field emission SEM instrument (Carl Zeiss SMTAG, Germany). For CuXO and CuXO/Cu chemical composition, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were carried out on a Kratos AXIS UltraDLD electron spectrometer with Al K X-ray anode source (hν = 1486.6eV) at 250 W and 14.0 kV. For analyzing product of CO2 electroreduction, the HCOO- concentrations were determined by ion chromatography (ICS-90, Dionex, USA) using an AS14 4 mm × 250 mm separation column at a flow rate of 1 ml/min. In this analysis, the mobile phase was the mixed aqueous solution of Na2CO3 (4.5 mM) and NaHCO3 (0.8 mM), and the H2SO4 (20 mM) aqueous solution was used as a regenerator.

sections.heading: 3.1 Morphology and composition of CuXO nanosphere particles
sections.text:
SEM and XRD were used to analyze the morphology and crystal structure (phase
composition) of the CuXO sample, respectively. For morphology of CuXO paprticles, Fig. 1(a) and (b) show the SEM images of the sample synthesized at 180oC for 2 hours. One can see that the sample was composed of 3-dimension (3D) hierarchical nanospheres with an average diameter of about 500 nm. Further from the high-resolution SEM image (Fig. 1(b)), it can be see that these nanospheres were comprised of secondary structures which are made up of laminated small nanosheets with an average diameter of about 50 nm. This special morphology formed may provide the catalysts large surface area and thus more active phases for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction as will be discussed below. The corresponding XRD AC CE

result shown in Fig. 1(c) indicates that these hierarchical nanospheres are the hybrids of CuO and Cu2O [13-15]. The diffraction peak centered at  42.2o is corresponding to cubic Cu2O while other peaks of XRD pattern show that most nanoparticles are monoclinic CuO [16-18]. Further by XPS analysis as shown in Fig. 2(a), the Cu 2p3/2 peaks also exhibit the known characteristics of CuO and Cu2O [19-21]. The main peak of CuO has a binding energy of 933.3±0.2 eV, and is accompanied by a satellite on the high binding energy side at about 941±0.2 and 943.4±0.2eV. The peak at 932.3±0.2 eV indicates the existence of Cu2O, which corresponds well with the XRD result. The atomic percentages of Cu(II) and Cu(I) in the sample were determined to be 74.7 at.% Cu(II) and 25.3 at% Cu(I) as shown in Fig. 2(d)), indicating that these hierarchical CuXO nanospheres are of 75.7 at.% CuO, and 25.3 at% Cu2O in composition. Fig. 2(b) shows the XPS spectrum of CuXO catalysts after CO2 reduction electrocatalysis at -1.1V vs. SHE for 20 hours. The atomic percentages of Cu(II) and hybrid Cu(I)/Cu(0) were calculated to be 68.1% at.% Cu(II) and 31.9 at% hybrid Cu(I)/Cu(0) (Fig. 2(d)). Since Cu(I) and Cu(0) has the same binding energy at 932.5±0.2 eV, LMM Auger spectra was used to confirm the existence of metal Cu. According to the literatures, the kinetic energy of Cu(I) is at about 916.6±0.2 eV, while the Cu(0) has a kinetic energy at about 918.2±0.2 eV [22,23]. As can be seen in Fig. 2(c), the kinetic energy of CuXO sample before electrolysis is at 916.8 eV, which rules out the existence of Cu(0). However, after 20 hours electrolysis the kinetic energy of CuXO sample shifts to 917.5 eV, indicating that there is a small amount of Cu(0) derived by the reduction of hierarchical CuXO nanosphere particles and, such Cu(0) could have a positive effect on the Faradaic efficiency of formate. This detailed Faradaic efficiency will be given in the following section.
To examine the active surface of the working electrode with coated hybrid
CuO-Cu2O hierarchical nanospheres, the double layer capacitance in N2-saturated 0.1 M HClO4 was measured by CV in a potential range without Faradaic process occurred. As shown in Fig. 3, the CV curves are recorded for both the GDL electrode without any catalyst (GDL) and that coated by CuXO nanospheres (CuXO/GDL). The

The capacitance of GDL electrode is about 170 μF cm-2, which is in accord with the published data on capacitance of carbon materials [24,25]. Under the same measuring conditions, however, the capacitance for the electrode of CuXO/GDL is nearly 800 μF cm-2, which is 4.7 times larger than the capacitance of GDL electrode. If the electrode of GDL is about 4 cm2, the CuXO/GDL electrode could be calculated to be 18.8 cm2 according to their surface capacitances [4,5]. Obviously, since these CuXO nanosphere particles have large surface area and special morphology, the enlarged capacitance is achieved due to the loading of CuXO hierarchical nanospheres which could provide more active sites for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction [26,27].

sections.heading: 3.2 Electrochemical redox reactions of CuXO nansphere particles

where the GDL electrode coated by this CuXO was measured by CV in the potential range between -1.2 and 1.2 V vs. SHE in CO2-satuarated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. There is a redox wave composed of an oxidation peak near 0.25 V and a reduction peak near -0.18 V, the average wave potential is about 0.035 V vs. SHE. It can be seen that a very good linear relationship was achieved, indicating the current is originated from the surface attached redox species.

As shown in Fig. 4, the CV curve of the CuXO/GDL electrode in CO2-saturated
0.5M KHCO3 electrolyte was carried out for examing the catalytic activity of CuXO/Cu catalyst for CO2 electroreduction. For a good comparison, the CV curve of bare GDL electrode was also provided in Fig. 4. It can be seen that a significant catalytic current for CO2 reduction was observed at about -0.25 V vs. SHE after the electrode is coated with hierarchical CuXO nanosphere particles. Without CuXO, a catalytic current was only observed starting from -0.5 V vs. SHE and the current was much smaller. For a more quantitative comparison, the current densities of CO2 reduction at a potential of -1.1 V vs. SHE in Fig. 4 are measured. It can be seen clearly that the value for bare GDL electrode is only about 1.5 mA cm-2, on the contrary, the coated GDL by hierarchical CuXO nanospheres can give a value of 10 mA cm-2, which is fifteen times enhanced compared to bare GDL electrode. This suggests that these CuXO nanospheres with special morphology have very strong activity for catalyzing the CO2 electroreduction. In Fig. 4, the CV curve using CuXO nanoparticle without 3D-hierarchical structure was also presented to verify further this morphology effect. As can be seen from Fig. 4, the on-set potential for the coated GDL by CuXO nanoparticle appeared at about -0.85 V vs. SHE, which are more 300 mV negative shift compared to that for the coated GDL by hierarchical CuXO nanospheres. The above result further demonstrates that the CuXO nanospheres with special hierarchical morphology could largely benefit the catalyzed CO2 activity. It should be mentioned that the overpotential for electrochemical CO2 reduction on this coated GDL by CuXO nanospheres is about -0.5 V vs. SHE, which is nearly 500 mV positive shift compared to the reported potential (-1.0 V vs. SHE) of metal Cu electrode [28]. In addition, Fig. 4 shows that the catalytic current can only start after CuXO was reduced to Cu (at the end of reduction peak at the negative potential direction in Fig. 4). It is supposed that metal Cu nanoparticle induced by the reduction of CuXO nanospheres could be an effective part participating in the catalytic reaction.

and C is total coulomb of electrons passed across the electrode of CuXO/GDL during the electrolysis. Fig. 6(a) shows the electrolysis time effect on Faradaic efficiency of formate at -1.1 V vs. SHE. When the electrolysis time is 30 min, the Faradaic efficiency of formate is only about 8.9%, however, along with the increase of electrolysis time to 5 hours, the Faradaic efficiency of formate sharply increased to 37%, and further reached high up to 62% resulted from the accumulation of Cu (0) when the electrolysis time was increased to 20 hours. Under this condition, the Faradaic efficiency of formate is about 1.7 times higher than the reported 33% on modified Cu electrodes (prepared by annealing Cu foil in air and electrochemically reducing the resulting Cu2O layers) [4] and 1.3 times higher than our most recent work of 43% [10] on fibrous Cu electrode surface created using a combined process of high-temperature annealing and electroreduction. These results clearly show that the CuXO/Cu catalyst, which induced from the CuXO nanosphere catalyst, is a very active CO2 reduction catalyst with high selectivity.
The potential profile for the Faradaic efficiency of formate can be seen in Fig.
6(b) that after 1 hour electrolysis, where the electrocatalysis was conducted at four different potentials. As can be seen in Fig. 6(b), both the Faradaic efficiency and current density increased as the potential decreased, reaching a maximum at -0.7 V vs. SHE. At -0.7 V the Faradaic efficiency of 59.3% with a current density of 2 mA cm-2 was obtained. For a good comparison, all the detailed Faradaic efficiencies are presented in Table 1. It is noted that the Faradaic efficiency of formate had reached 42.4% after electrolysis of CO2 at the overpotential of only -0.5 V vs. SHE for 1 hour (Table 1), while at more negatively applied potentials, for example, at -1.1 V, the Faradaic efficiency of formate sharply decreased to 8.4%. The Tafel slope obtained from CuXO(hierarchical nanosphere)/GDL electrode is 240 mV dec-1, which is about 15 mV dec-1 less than the 265 mV dec-1 obtained from GDL electrode, about 45 mV dec-1 less than that of CuXO (nanoparticle)/GDL electrode and nearly ～150 mV dec-1 less than that of reported metallic Cu electrode [7]. This result indicates that the rate-determining step of CO2 electroreduction catalyzed by CuXO nanosphere particle catalyst has a higher electron transfer coefficient than that of electrode without CuXO catalyst, as calculated by Equation (5). By Comparing the oi value (1.6 × 10 -5 A cm-2) obtained using CuXO/GDL electrode with that observed using Cu2O film based Cu electrode (~10-10 A cm-2) [4], the value of obtained is five orders higher. Further according to the literature [31], the exchange current density of the reduction of Cu2O to Cu (~1.7× 10-8) is about 3 orders lower than that of the CuXO (hierarchical nanosphere)/GDL electrode reported in this paper. For the metallic Cu electrode reported elsewhere [7], the exchange current density of Cu (~1.9 × 10-4) is about ten times higher than that of CuXO (hierarchical nanosphere)/GDL electrode, however, the Tafel slope (~390 mVdec-1) of metallic Cu in CO2 reduction is about 1.6 times higher. This suggests that the CuXO/Cu composite is the main catalytic part as observed by XPS tests during the cathodic reduction process (Fig. 3).

sections.heading: 3.5 Stability of CuXO/Cu catalyst in CO2 electroreduction
sections.text:
To test the stability of CuXO/Cu catalyst in CO2 electroreduction, a piece of 4
cm-2 GDL was used as an electrode to support 15 mg CuXO nanosphere particles (about 80% CuXO was coated on), the loading of which was 3 mg cm-2, and was measured 20 hours in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. The test was performed potentiostatically at a constant potential of -1.1 V vs. SHE. Fig. 8 shows the

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this work, novel 3-dimension hierarchical CuXO nanosphere particles are
synthesized using a simple hydro-thermal method. The morphology, composition, crystal structure and surface area of these CuXO nanosphere particles are characterized using SEM, XRD, XPS as well as surface cyclic voltammetry. These CuXO nanosphere particles are found to be made of number of small nanosheets. The chemical compositions of these CuXO nanosphere particles are analyzed to be a mixture of CuO and Cu2O. The electrochemical redox processes of this CuXO particle to form metal Cu particle is also studied by cyclic voltammetry, and its corresponding reactions are identified.
The hierarchically structured CuXO nanospheres are used as the catalyst for CO2
electroreduction, and we demonstrate here the remarkable observation of selective reduction of CO2 to formate in 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous electrolyte. It is found that this induced CuXO/Cu catalyst has both high activity and high selectivity with a ~62% of Faradaic efficiency of formate production. The catalyst stability is also tested with a 20 h of electrolysis at a constant electrode potential of -1.1 V vs. SHE in the presence of CO2, no any degradation can be observed in such a period, indicating that this CuXO/Cu catalyst is stable for CO2 electroreduction.
